claim: Small molecules such as cyanine 3 (Cy3) and 4-hydroxy-3-nitrophenylacetyl (NP) are γδ T cell antigens recognized directly by specific γδ TCRs.
source: Here we report that small molecules, such as cyanine 3 (Cy3), a synthetic fluorescent molecule, and 4-hydroxy-3-nitrophenylacetyl (NP), one of the most noted haptens, are γδ T cell antigens, recognized directly by specific γδ TCRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including FACS analysis, surface plasmon resonance, and functional assays demonstrating direct recognition.

claim: Immunization with Cy3 conjugates induces a rapid Cy3-specific γδ T cell IL-17 response.
source: Immunization with Cy3 conjugates induces a rapid Cy3-specific γδ T cell IL-17 response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing IL-17 production by Cy3-specific γδ T cells after immunization with Cy3-CGG.

claim: γδ T cells couple B cell-like antigen recognition capability with T cell effector function.
source: These results expand the role of small molecules and chemical modifications in immunity and underscore the role of γδ T cells as unique adaptive immune cells that couple B cell-like antigen recognition capability with T cell effector function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the demonstrated ability of γδ T cells to recognize small molecules (like B cells) while producing T cell cytokines like IL-17.

claim: γδ T cells and αβ T cells are present together in all but the most primitive vertebrates.
source: While αβ T cells perform all well-defined functions attributed to T cells, γδ T cells and αβ T cells are present together in all but the most primitive vertebrates.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about the evolutionary conservation of T cell subsets.

claim: γδ T cells and αβ T cells differ in their antigen recognition and activation requirements.
source: Indeed, although γδ T cells and αβ T cells have similar effector functions, γδ T cells and αβ T cells are distinct in their antigen recognition and activation requirements and in their antigen-specific repertoire and effector function development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article (Chien et al., 2014) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Haptens are small organic molecules which, when conjugated to a protein, induce a strong hapten-specific B cell response.
source: Haptens were characterized as small organic molecules which, when conjugated to a protein, induce a strong hapten-specific B cell response.
evidence: The claim is supported by historical citations (Landsteiner and van der Scheer, 1931; Landsteiner and Chase, 1937) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Antibody responses to haptens have been used extensively to investigate antibody affinity maturation, germinal center formation, and the development of memory B cell responses.
source: Since then, antibody responses to haptens have been used extensively to investigate antibody affinity maturation, germinal center formation, and the development of memory B cell responses (Jack et al., 1977; Jacob et al., 1991; McHeyzer-Williams and McHeyzer-Williams, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the use of haptens in immunological research.

claim: Antibodies specific for pathogen-produced small compounds and chemical modifications of host molecules serve as a means of pathogen surveillance.
source: Antibodies specific for pathogen-produced small compounds and chemical modifications of host molecules have also served as a means of pathogen surveillance (Daneshvar et al., 1989; Temmerman et al., 2004) and to monitor injury or altered physiological states (Vossenaar et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2006; Yang and Sauve, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this surveillance function.

claim: Interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and hapten ligands has not been demonstrated for hapten-specific αβ T cells.
source: Although hapten-specific αβ T cells have been reported and studied in the context of suppressor T cell function, as exemplified by the work of Dorf et al. (Sherr and Dorf, 1981), interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and the hapten ligand has not been demonstrated.
evidence: The claim is based on a citation and the absence of evidence in the literature for direct TCR-hapten interaction in αβ T cells.

claim: The antigen-specific repertoires of peripheral αβ T cells are largely limited to peptides that are processed from protein antigens in complex with the host major histocompatability complex (MHC) molecules.
source: Moreover, it is well established that the antigen-specific repertoires of peripheral αβ T cells are largely limited to peptides that are processed from protein antigens in complex with the host major histocompatability complex (MHC) molecules (Huseby et al., 2005; Van Laethem et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about αβ T cell antigen recognition.

claim: The restriction on αβ T cell antigen specificity is a consequence of the thymic development process.
source: This restriction on antigen specificity is a consequence of the thymic development process (Van Laethem et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation documenting the role of thymic selection in shaping αβ T cell repertoires.

claim: Adaptive immune recognition of small molecules is mainly mediated by B cells rather than T cells.
source: Thus, adaptive immune recognition of small molecules seems to be mainly mediated by B cells rather than T cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the established knowledge about αβ T cell MHC restriction and the lack of demonstrated direct hapten recognition by T cells.

claim: γδ T cells require thymic maturation before entering the periphery.
source: While γδ T cells, like αβ T cells, require thymic maturation before entering the periphery (Ohno et al., 1993), this process does little to constrain the γδ T cell antigen-specific repertoire (Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating thymic maturation requirements for γδ T cells.

claim: Thymic maturation does little to constrain the γδ T cell antigen-specific repertoire.
source: While γδ T cells, like αβ T cells, require thymic maturation before entering the periphery (Ohno et al., 1993), this process does little to constrain the γδ T cell antigen-specific repertoire (Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study examining γδ T cell repertoire development.

claim: Adult human and murine γδ T cells in blood, lymph node, spleen, and intestine express diverse TCRs.
source: In addition, although fetal-derived γδ T cells in murine skin and the reproductive tract express non-variant TCRs, adult human and murine γδ T cells in other lymphoid compartments (blood, lymph node, spleen, and intestine) express diverse TCRs (Chien et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article summarizing knowledge about γδ T cell TCR diversity.

claim: γδ TCRs are more similar to immunoglobulins (Igs) than to αβ TCRs based on CDR3 sequence diversity and length distribution.
source: Analysis of γδ TCR CDR3 sequence diversity and length distribution suggest that these T cells have extensive antigen recognition capability and that as a group, γδ TCRs are more similar to immunoglobulins (Igs) than to αβ TCRs (Rock et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study analyzing γδ TCR sequence characteristics.

claim: The requirements of γδ T cell antigen recognition are similar to those of B cells.
source: Since the requirements of γδ T cell antigen recognition are similar to those of B cells, we investigated whether γδ T cells, like B cells, can recognize haptens.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity in TCR structure and diversity between γδ TCRs and immunoglobulins.

claim: Cy3 tetramer stained approximately 0.05-0.2% of normal splenic γδ T cells.
source: Cy3 tetramer (Cy34SAv) (a recombinant mutant of streptavidin (Ramachandiran et al., 2007) labeled with four Cy3 molecules at the C-terminal cysteine in each of the four identical subunits) stained ∼0.05–0.2% of normal splenic γδ T cells, but not G8/Rag2−/− γδ TCR transgenic cells (specific for the nonclassical MHC class I T10 and T22) (Bluestone et al., 1988; Schild et al., 1994; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating Cy3 tetramer staining of splenic γδ T cells.

claim: Cy3 tetramer did not stain G8/Rag2−/− γδ TCR transgenic cells.
source: Cy3 tetramer (Cy34SAv) (a recombinant mutant of streptavidin (Ramachandiran et al., 2007) labeled with four Cy3 molecules at the C-terminal cysteine in each of the four identical subunits) stained ∼0.05–0.2% of normal splenic γδ T cells, but not G8/Rag2−/− γδ TCR transgenic cells (specific for the nonclassical MHC class I T10 and T22) (Bluestone et al., 1988; Schild et al., 1994; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating lack of Cy3 tetramer staining of G8/Rag2−/− cells.

claim: 58α-β- cells expressing Cy3-specific γδ TCRs bound Cy3-ovalbumin, Cy3-BSA, and Cy3-MCC-streptavidin, but not FITC or APC labeled OVA, nor PE-MCC peptide/streptavidin.
source: 58α-β- cells expressing Cy3-specific γδ TCRs bound Cy3-ovalbumin (Cy3-OVA), Cy3-bovine serum albumin (Cy3-BSA), Cy3-MCC-streptavidin (moth cytochrome C (MCC)-derived peptide, Cy3-labeled at the N-terminus, biotinylated at the C-terminus, and tetramerized with streptavidin), but not FITC or APC labeled OVA, nor PE-MCC peptide/streptavidin (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrating specific binding to Cy3-conjugated proteins.

claim: Cy3-MCC-streptavidin staining of NX6/58α-β- cells was inhibited by Fab fragments of an anti-Cy3 antibody.
source: Moreover, Cy3-MCC-streptavidin staining of a Cy3-specific γδ TCR NX6/58α-β- was inhibited by the inclusion of Fab fragments of an anti-Cy3 antibody (clone A-6; Santa Cruz Biotechnology) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating blocking of Cy3 staining by anti-Cy3 Fab.

claim: NX6/58α-β- cells were activated by plate-bound Cy3-OVA, but not unmodified OVA.
source: In addition, NX6/58α-β- cells were activated by plate-bound Cy3-OVA, but not unmodified OVA (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by IL-2 production data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating functional activation by Cy3-conjugated protein.

claim: The soluble form of Cy3-specific γδ TCR (NX6) binds to Cy34SAv with an apparent KD of 78.2 nM as measured by surface plasmon resonance.
source: Binding of the soluble form of a Cy3-specific γδ TCR (NX6) to Cy34SAv can be demonstrated by surface plasmon resonance (Biacore) with an apparent KD of 78.2 nM (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface plasmon resonance data shown in Figure 1F measuring binding affinity.

claim: Cy34SAv binding to NX6 expressed on 58α-β- cells has an apparent KD of 1.8 nM with a half-life of approximately 26 minutes.
source: We also examined the affinity of Cy34SAv binding to NX6 expressed on 58α-β- cells. Scatchard analysis showed an apparent nanomolar KD (1.8 nM) with a half-life of ∼26 min (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Scatchard analysis and kinetic data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Prior to immunization, approximately 80% of Cy3-specific γδ T cells in the lymph nodes were CD44lo.
source: We found that prior to immunization, ∼80% of Cy3-specific γδ T cells in the lymph nodes were CD44lo, a phenotype typical of naïve T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analyzing CD44 expression on Cy3-specific γδ T cells before immunization.

claim: Within 24 hours after immunization, Cy3-specific γδ T cells up-regulated CD44 in Cy3-CGG-immunized mice, but not in CGG-immunized mice.
source: Within 24 hr after immunization, Cy3-specific γδ T cells up-regulated CD44 in Cy3-CGG-immunized mice, but not in CGG-immunized mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating CD44 upregulation after Cy3-CGG immunization.

claim: Cy3-specific γδ T cells express mRNA coding for RORγt, IL-17A and IL-17F 60 hours after immunization.
source: BioMark analysis showed that Cy3-specific γδ T cells express the mRNA coding for RORγt, IL-17A and IL-17F 60 hr after immunization (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by BioMark gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 60 hours after Cy3-CGG immunization, activated Cy3-specific γδ T cells expressed the Thy1.1 reporter or IL-17 protein in IL-17F reporter mice.
source: Consistent with this observation, analysis of Cy3-specific γδ T cell responses in IL-17F reporter mice (Il-17fThy1.1/Thy1.1) (Lee et al., 2009) and staining showed that 60 hr after Cy3-CGG immunization, activated Cy3-specific γδ T cells expressed the Thy1.1 reporter or IL-17 protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data from IL-17F reporter mice shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Activated Cy3-specific γδ T cells expressed receptors for IL-1 and IL-23.
source: In addition, we found that activated Cy3-specific γδ T cells expressed the receptors for IL-1 and IL-23 (Figure 2B), a characteristic similar to our analysis of activated PE-specific γδ T cells in an immune response (Zeng et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by BioMark gene expression data shown in Figure 2B and comparison to previous findings.

claim: Expression of inflammatory cytokine receptors allows antigen-activated γδ T cells to integrate signals from antigen receptors and cytokine receptors to mount an enhanced and sustained response.
source: The expression of inflammatory cytokine receptors allows antigen-activated γδ T cells to integrate signals from antigen receptors and cytokine receptors to mount an enhanced and sustained response (Zeng et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: NP-PE stained approximately 0.14% of splenic γδ T cells of normal mice.
source: We found that NP-PE stained ∼0.14% of splenic γδ T cells of normal mice (left panel), but not G8/Rag2−/− γδ TCR transgenic cells (middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B demonstrating NP-PE staining of splenic γδ T cells.

claim: PE stained approximately 0.03% of splenic γδ T cells under the same staining conditions.
source: Consistent with the observation that PE is a γδ T cell antigen (Zeng et al., 2012), we found ∼0.03% of splenic γδ T cells stained with PE under the same staining conditions (right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to previous work identifying PE as a γδ T cell antigen.

claim: Approximately 0.1% of total γδ T cells are NP-specific after accounting for background and PE staining.
source: After accounting for background staining and for PE staining, we estimated that ∼0.1% of total γδ T cells could be NP-specific (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FACS data shown in Figure 3B by subtracting PE-specific cells from NP-PE staining.

claim: 58α-β- cells expressing NP-specific γδ TCRs can be stained with NP-CGG-Cy5, but not CGG-Cy5.
source: Expressing NP-specific γδ TCRs in 58α-β- cells enables these cells to be stained with NP-CGG-Cy5, but not CGG-Cy5 (Figure 3C; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating specific binding to NP-conjugated protein.

claim: 58α-β- cells expressing NP-specific γδ TCRs can be stained with NP-BSA-Cy5 and NP-PE, but not with BSA-Cy5 or PE.
source: Further investigation showed 58α-β- cells expressing NP-specific γδ TCRs could also be stained with NP-BSA-Cy5 and NP-PE, but not with BSA-Cy5 or PE (Figure 3D, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3D demonstrating specific binding to NP-conjugated proteins.

claim: NP-PE staining of NP-specific γδ TCR-expressing cells was inhibited by Fab fragments of an anti-NP antibody.
source: In addition, NP-PE staining was inhibited by the inclusion of Fab fragments of an anti-NP antibody (clone H33Lγ; G. Kelsoe) (Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3D demonstrating blocking of NP staining by anti-NP Fab.

claim: 58α-β- cells expressing NP-specific γδ TCRs produced IL-2 in response to plate-bound NP-KLH, but not plate-bound KLH in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, 58α-β- cells expressing NP-specific γδ TCRs produced IL-2 in response to plate-bound NP-keyhole limpet hemocyanin (NP-KLH), but not plate-bound KLH in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by IL-2 production data shown in Figure 3E demonstrating functional activation by NP-conjugated protein.

claim: The measured apparent KD for the interaction between NP43-CGG and the 1G9 TCR was 0.66 μM.
source: The measured apparent KD for the interaction between NP43-CGG and the 1G9 TCR was 0.66 μM.
evidence: The claim is supported by surface plasmon resonance data shown in Figure 3F measuring binding affinity.

claim: NP43-CGG exhibited no binding to the PE-specific γδ TCR, MA2.
source: NP43-CGG exhibited no binding to the PE-specific γδ TCR, MA2 (Zeng et al., 2012), and CGG did not bind 1G9 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface plasmon resonance data shown in Figure 3F demonstrating specificity of binding.

claim: CGG did not bind the NP-specific TCR 1G9.
source: NP43-CGG exhibited no binding to the PE-specific γδ TCR, MA2 (Zeng et al., 2012), and CGG did not bind 1G9 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface plasmon resonance data shown in Figure 3F demonstrating specificity of binding.

claim: This is the first demonstration that γδ TCRs can interact directly with small molecules.
source: This is the first demonstration that γδ TCRs can interact directly with small molecules.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript and the absence of prior reports.

claim: A collection of small pyrophosphate-containing organic molecules can stimulate human Vγ9Vδ2-expressing γδ T cells in vitro in a TCR-dependent manner.
source: In this context, prior work has shown that a collection of small pyrophosphate-containing organic molecules can stimulate human Vγ9Vδ2-expressing γδ T cells (also referred to as Vγ2Vδ2 by the Seidman et al. nomenclature) in vitro in a TCR-dependent manner (Chien et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article summarizing prior work on phosphoantigen recognition.

claim: Phosphoantigens do not interact directly with the γδ TCR.
source: However, recent reports indicate that pAgs do not interact directly with the γδ TCR.
evidence: The claim is based on recent reports cited in the manuscript showing indirect recognition mechanisms.

claim: Vγ9Vδ2 T cell activation by phosphoantigens is through the recognition of an allosteric change in the extracellular domain of butyrophilin 3A1, which is induced in response to intracellular accumulation of phosphoantigen.
source: Instead, Vγ9Vδ2 T cell activation by pAgs is through the recognition of an allosteric change in the extracellular domain of a cell surface molecule, butyrophilin 3A1, which is induced in response to intracellular accumulation of pAg (Wang et al., 2013; Sandstrom et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies elucidating the mechanism of phosphoantigen recognition.

claim: γδ T cells need not encounter cognate antigen in the thymus to signal through the TCR, mature, and exit to the periphery.
source: Our past studies indicate that γδ T cells need not encounter cognate antigen in the thymus to signal through the TCR, mature, and exit to the periphery.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous studies on γδ T cell development.

claim: Peripheral γδ T cells derived from γδ thymocytes that have not previously encountered thymic ligands produce IL-17 upon TCR triggering.
source: Peripheral γδ T cells derived from γδ thymocytes that have not previously encountered thymic ligands produce IL-17 upon TCR triggering (Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating IL-17 production by γδ T cells without prior thymic antigen encounter.

claim: Phycoerytherin (PE) is a member of the phycobiliprotein family, which is located on the tip of photosynthetic antenna of red algae and cyanobacteria.
source: Indeed, we have identified multiple foreign molecules which are γδ T cell antigens: phycoerytherin (PE), a member of the phycobiliprotein family, which is located on the tip of photosynthetic antenna of red algae and cyanobacteria (Zeng et al., 2012), and here, the haptens Cy3 and NP as γδ T cell antigens.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the structure and location of phycoerythrin.

claim: Both Cy3 and PE-specific γδ T cells differentiate toward an IL-17-producing phenotype with similar activation kinetics upon antigen encounter.
source: Moreover, both Cy3 and PE-specific γδ T cells differentiate toward an IL-17-producing phenotype with similar activation kinetics upon antigen encounter (Zeng et al., 2012) (and this manuscript): within 24 hr after immunization, PE- or Cy3 specific γδ T cells in the draining lymph node showed activated phenotypes, such as becoming CD44hi and CD62Llo.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current manuscript and a citation to previous work on PE-specific γδ T cells.

claim: Within 24 hours after immunization, PE- or Cy3 specific γδ T cells in the draining lymph node showed activated phenotypes, such as becoming CD44hi and CD62Llo.
source: Moreover, both Cy3 and PE-specific γδ T cells differentiate toward an IL-17-producing phenotype with similar activation kinetics upon antigen encounter (Zeng et al., 2012) (and this manuscript): within 24 hr after immunization, PE- or Cy3 specific γδ T cells in the draining lymph node showed activated phenotypes, such as becoming CD44hi and CD62Llo.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current manuscript showing CD44 and CD62L expression changes.

claim: Activated antigen-specific γδ T cells express RORγt 48 hours after immunization.
source: Activated antigen-specific γδ T cells express RORγt 48 hr after immunization and, after another 12 hr, IL-17A and IL-17F.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from the manuscript showing temporal expression patterns.

claim: Activated antigen-specific γδ T cells express IL-17A and IL-17F 60 hours after immunization.
source: Activated antigen-specific γδ T cells express RORγt 48 hr after immunization and, after another 12 hr, IL-17A and IL-17F.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from the manuscript showing temporal expression patterns.

claim: The expression of inflammatory cytokine receptors such as IL-1R and IL-23R are induced on antigen activated γδ T cells.
source: Significantly, the expression of inflammatory cytokine receptors such as IL-1R and IL-23R are induced on antigen activated γδ T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cytokine-receptor signaling provides a 'second signal' in addition to TCR engagement to perpetuate the response in inflammation.
source: The cytokine-receptor signaling provides a 'second signal' in addition to TCR engagement to perpetuate the response in inflammation (Zeng et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: The inflammatory response is an essential mechanism in the host response to infection and injury.
source: The inflammatory response is an essential mechanism in the host response to infection and injury.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the role of inflammation in immunity.

claim: In vertebrates, the inflammatory response requires IL-17, a cytokine primarily made by T cells.
source: In vertebrates, it requires IL-17, a cytokine primarily made by T cells.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about IL-17 production and its role in inflammation.

claim: IL-17 induces the maturation and release of neutrophils from the bone marrow.
source: IL-17 induces the maturation and release of neutrophils from the bone marrow (Stark et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation documenting the role of IL-17 in neutrophil biology.

claim: Neutrophil infiltration focuses the immune response at the site of infection or injury.
source: Neutrophil infiltration focuses the immune response at the site of infection or injury, where antigen-specific αβ T cells subsequently proliferate and gain effector functions after stimulation by professional antigen-presenting cells and a particular cytokine environment.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the role of neutrophils in immune responses.

claim: In acute infection, the host must make IL-17 rapidly without prior antigen exposure.
source: In acute infection, the host must make IL-17 rapidly without prior antigen exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement for rapid inflammatory responses in acute infection.

claim: γδ T cells are uniquely suited for the initial IL-17 response.
source: The results presented here, together with our previous studies, suggest that γδ T cells are uniquely suited for the initial IL-17 response and provide a way for haptens to elicit this important T cell response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing rapid IL-17 production by hapten-specific γδ T cells and previous studies.

claim: Haptenation enhances the immunogenicity of the carrier protein independent of innate immune recognition and signaling.
source: In this context, it has been noted that haptenation enhances the immunogenicity of the carrier protein, but this effect is independent of innate immune recognition and signaling (Palm and Medzhitov, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study examining the mechanism of hapten-enhanced immunogenicity.

claim: The synthetic hapten molecule NP is structurally similar to nitrated tyrosine (3-NTyr).
source: The synthetic hapten molecule NP is structurally similar to nitrated tyrosine (3-NTyr).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison of the two molecules.

claim: 3-NTyr-containing proteins are formed in the presence of peroxynitrite, one of the side products of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species produced during the early stages of inflammation.
source: 3-NTyr-containing proteins are formed in the presence of peroxynitrite, one of the side products of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species produced during the early stages of inflammation (Beckman et al., 1992; Ischiropoulos et al., 1992a; Ischiropoulos et al., 1992b; Beckmann et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the formation of nitrated tyrosine during inflammation.

claim: Tyrosine nitration has been demonstrated in Trypanosoma cruzi infection and atherosclerosis.
source: Tyrosine nitration has been demonstrated in a variety of infectious and inflammatory contexts, such as Trypanosoma cruzi infection (Naviliat et al., 2005; Dhiman et al., 2008) and atherosclerosis (Beckmann et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating tyrosine nitration in these disease contexts.

claim: Trypanosoma cruzi infection and atherosclerosis are driven in part by IL-17 and γδ T cells.
source: There have been reports indicating that these pathological processes are driven in part by IL-17 and γδ T cells (Stemme et al., 1991; Kleindienst et al., 1993; Lima and Titus, 1996; Hashmi and Zeng, 2006; Sardinha et al., 2006; Cheng et al., 2008; van Es et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the role of IL-17 and γδ T cells in these diseases.

claim: The synthetic hapten molecule Cy3 contains two modified indole groups joined by polymethine bonds.
source: Furthermore, the synthetic hapten molecule Cy3 contains two modified indole groups joined by polymethine bonds.
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical structure of Cy3 shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The indole molecule is a noted bacterial product and signaling molecule, which accumulates at the site of bacterial infection and affects antibiotic resistance and other virulence factors.
source: The indole molecule is a noted bacterial product and signaling molecule, which accumulates at the site of bacterial infection and affects antibiotic resistance and other virulence factors (Martino et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2007; Hirakawa et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the role of indole in bacterial biology.

claim: An indole group forms the side chain of tryptophan.
source: An indole group also forms the side chain of tryptophan.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about amino acid structure.

claim: Altered tryptophan metabolism along the kynurenine pathway and an unrestrained γδ T cell IL-17 response were identified as the causes of lethal pulmonary aspergillosis in a mouse model of chronic granulomatous disease.
source: Altered tryptophan metabolism along the kynurenine pathway and an unrestrained γδ T cell IL-17 response were identified as the causes of lethal pulmonary aspergillosis in a mouse model of chronic granulomatous disease (Romani et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study identifying these mechanisms in aspergillosis.

claim: Small molecules and chemical modifications on proteins are γδ T cell targets.
source: Regardless, our observations that small molecules and chemical modifications on proteins are γδ T cell targets suggest a new category of antigen specificity in addition to cell surface molecules such as the non-classical MHC class I molecules T10 and T22, MHC class I-related chain A/B (MICA/B), and endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) (Willcox et al., 2012) that can activate γδ T cells in infection and inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript demonstrating recognition of haptens by γδ T cells.

claim: Non-classical MHC class I molecules T10 and T22, MHC class I-related chain A/B (MICA/B), and endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) are cell surface molecules that can activate γδ T cells in infection and inflammation.
source: Regardless, our observations that small molecules and chemical modifications on proteins are γδ T cell targets suggest a new category of antigen specificity in addition to cell surface molecules such as the non-classical MHC class I molecules T10 and T22, MHC class I-related chain A/B (MICA/B), and endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) (Willcox et al., 2012) that can activate γδ T cells in infection and inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review documenting these known γδ T cell antigens.

claim: γδ T cells have been implicated in mouse models of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD).
source: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) represents a specific example of a delayed-type-hypersensitivity response with a hapten-driven mechanism. γδ T cells have been implicated in mouse models of ACD.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the role of γδ T cells in ACD models.

claim: Some studies suggest that γδ T cells assist αβ T cells in adoptive transfer of contact sensitivity.
source: Some studies suggest that γδ T cells assist αβ T cells in adoptive transfer of contact sensitivity (Ptak and Askenase, 1992), while others suggest that γδ T cells regulate effector αβ T cell responses (Guan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study showing this assisting role.

claim: Some studies suggest that γδ T cells regulate effector αβ T cell responses in allergic contact dermatitis.
source: Some studies suggest that γδ T cells assist αβ T cells in adoptive transfer of contact sensitivity (Ptak and Askenase, 1992), while others suggest that γδ T cells regulate effector αβ T cell responses (Guan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study showing this regulatory role.

claim: Only αβ T cells that can recognize proteins that are internalized and presented by B cells and displayed as peptide/MHC complexes on cell surface can provide B cell help.
source: This is best illustrated in αβ T cell-dependent antibody responses, wherein only αβ T cells that can recognize proteins that are internalized and presented by B cells and displayed as peptide/MHC complexes on cell surface can provide B cell help.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about T cell-B cell interactions in antibody responses.

claim: Only haptens coupled to proteins, which can be processed and presented for αβ T cell recognition, can induce a hapten-specific antibody response.
source: Thus, only haptens coupled to proteins, which can be processed and presented for αβ T cell recognition, can induce a hapten-specific antibody response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement for αβ T cell help in antibody responses and the MHC restriction of αβ T cells.

claim: αβ T cells are responsible for the development of high affinity, isotype-switched antibodies.
source: While αβ T cells are responsible for the development of high affinity, isotype-switched antibodies, we found that γδ T cells recognize and respond to noted B cell antigens such as PE, NP and Cy3.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the role of T cell help in antibody maturation.

claim: In a case of human autoimmune myositis with clonally expanded γδ T cells that destroy muscle fiber, the targets of γδ T cells were also the targets of autoantibodies known as anti-Jo-1.
source: In addition, in a case of human autoimmune myositis, where clonally expanded γδ T cells destroy muscle fiber, the targets of γδ T cells were also the targets of autoantibodies known as anti-Jo-1 (Bruder et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this overlap in antigen recognition.

claim: There is an overlap between the γδ T cell and B cell antigen-specific repertoires.
source: These observations indicate that an overlap between the γδ T cell and B cell antigen-specific repertoires.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that γδ T cells recognize PE, NP, Cy3, and anti-Jo-1 antigens, which are also B cell antigens.

claim: The size of the B cell antigen-specific repertoire was estimated as roughly 10^5 based on antigen-specific B cell frequencies of 0.004-0.007% for nitrophenyl (NP), dinitrophenyl (DNP), and trinitrophenyl (TNP).
source: The size of the B cell antigen-specific repertoire was estimated as roughly 105, based largely on antigen-specific B cell frequencies of 0.004–0.007% for nitrophenyl (NP), dinitrophenyl (DNP), and trinitrophenyl (TNP). These values were obtained using antigen-specific spleen foci formation, (Press and Klinman, 1974; Stashenko and Klinman, 1980) and are likely to be underestimates, as this assay requires extensive proliferation of individual clones.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to studies that estimated B cell repertoire size using spleen foci formation assays.

claim: In naïve mice, 0.1% of the B cells are PE-specific and 0.02% are allophycocyanin (APC)-specific.
source: In fact, FACS analysis showed that in naïve mice, 0.1% of the B cells are PE-specific and 0.02% allophycocyanin (APC)-specific (Pape et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study using FACS to measure antigen-specific B cell frequencies.

claim: Using PE and APC-specific B cell frequencies, the size of the antigen-specific B cell repertoire would be approximately 1000-5000, in the same range as that estimated for γδ T cells.
source: Using these values, the size of the antigen-specific B cell repertoire would be ∼1000–5000, in the same range as that estimated for γδ T cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FACS-based B cell frequencies and comparison to γδ T cell frequencies.

claim: If the frequencies of other antigen-specific γδ T cells were in a similar range as that of PE, Cy3 and NP, then the numbers of distinct γδ T cell antigens would be approximately 10^3-10^4.
source: If the frequencies of other antigen-specific γδ T cells were also in a similar range as that of PE, Cy3 and NP, then the numbers of distinct γδ T cell antigens would be ∼103–104.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the measured frequencies of PE, Cy3, and NP-specific γδ T cells.

claim: γδ T cells and B cells can recognise the same antigen.
source: Regardless of the extent of overlap between B cell and γδ T cell antigen-specific repertoires, our results here support previous observations (Bruder et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2012) that γδ T cells and β cells can recognise the same antigen.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current manuscript and citations to previous studies showing shared antigen recognition.

claim: NP and PE have been used extensively as model antigens to elucidate principles of antibody affinity maturation, germinal center formation and the development of memory B cell responses.
source: In particular, NP- and PE have been used extensively as model antigens to elucidate principles of antibody affinity maturation, germinal center formation and the development of memory B cell responses.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the use of these antigens in immunological research.

claim: Alum is a non-antigenic adjuvant.
source: Alum was used because it is a non-antigenic adjuvant (Eisenbarth et al., 2008), and we chose subcutaneous immunization because it focuses the immune response to the draining lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation documenting the properties of alum as an adjuvant.

claim: Subcutaneous immunization focuses the immune response to the draining lymph nodes.
source: Alum was used because it is a non-antigenic adjuvant (Eisenbarth et al., 2008), and we chose subcutaneous immunization because it focuses the immune response to the draining lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the route of immunization and immune response localization.

claim: Cy3 is a synthetic dye with two modified indole groups joined by a polymethine chain.
source: Cy3 is a synthetic dye with two modified indole groups joined by a polymethine chain (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical structure shown in Figure 1A and established knowledge about Cy3 structure.

claim: Cy3 is highly fluorescent and can be used for FACS analysis directly.
source: It is highly fluorescent and can be used for FACS analysis directly.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about the fluorescent properties of Cy3.

claim: G8/Rag2−/− γδ TCR transgenic cells are specific for the nonclassical MHC class I T10 and T22.
source: Cy3 tetramer (Cy34SAv) (a recombinant mutant of streptavidin (Ramachandiran et al., 2007) labeled with four Cy3 molecules at the C-terminal cysteine in each of the four identical subunits) stained ∼0.05–0.2% of normal splenic γδ T cells, but not G8/Rag2−/− γδ TCR transgenic cells (specific for the nonclassical MHC class I T10 and T22) (Bluestone et al., 1988; Schild et al., 1994; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting the specificity of the G8 TCR transgenic cells.

claim: CD44lo is a phenotype typical of naïve T cells.
source: We found that prior to immunization, ∼80% of Cy3-specific γδ T cells in the lymph nodes were CD44lo, a phenotype typical of naïve T cells.
evidence: The claim draws from established knowledge about CD44 expression as a marker of T cell activation status.

claim: PE is a γδ T cell antigen.
source: Consistent with the observation that PE is a γδ T cell antigen (Zeng et al., 2012), we found ∼0.03% of splenic γδ T cells stained with PE under the same staining conditions (right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study identifying PE as a γδ T cell antigen.

claim: High affinity, isotype-switched Cy3-specific antibodies are widely available commercially.
source: Although Cy3 has not been used in this context previously, high affinity, isotype-switched Cy3-specific antibodies are widely available commercially, indicating that Cy3 is also highly immunogenic, similar to other well-studied hapten molecules.
evidence: The claim is based on the commercial availability of anti-Cy3 antibodies, which indicates prior immunization and antibody production.

claim: Cy3 is highly immunogenic, similar to other well-studied hapten molecules.
source: Although Cy3 has not been used in this context previously, high affinity, isotype-switched Cy3-specific antibodies are widely available commercially, indicating that Cy3 is also highly immunogenic, similar to other well-studied hapten molecules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the commercial availability of high-affinity, isotype-switched anti-Cy3 antibodies.
